Floor
FLOR
n.
Old English flor. Webster 1828: that part of a building on which we walk; also, a threshing floor, a level area for treading out grain. In the Authorized Version the second sense carries most of the weight: the threshingfloor is where grain is separated from chaff, and it becomes a figure of judgment.

Biblical Definition

The floor in Scripture is usually a threshingfloor, a hard level place where the harvest is beaten and winnowed. It stands for the yield of a man’s labour: a released servant is to be furnished out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress (Deuteronomy 15:14). It is where Ruth goes at Naomi’s direction — get thee down to the floor (Ruth 3:3) — and where Boaz, guarding her reputation as carefully as her claim, says Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor (Ruth 3:14). It also names the literal floor of holy places: dust that is in the floor of the tabernacle was used in the trial of jealousy (Numbers 5:17), and Solomon overlaid the floor of the house with gold, within and without (1 Kings 6:30). But the figure that governs is John the Baptist’s. Of the Coming One he says, Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matthew 3:12). The threshingfloor is the visible church and the world alike, wheat and chaff lying together until the winnowing fan comes into a hand that will not tire.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives FLOOR as that part of a building or room on which we walk; and, secondly, a platform of boards or planks laid on timbers, as also the pavement or level area on which grain is threshed. Scripture uses both.

expand to see more

FLOOR, n. — That part of a building or room on which we walk; the bottom or lower part, consisting of boards, planks or pavement.

A platform of boards or planks laid on timbers, as in a bridge; also, the area on which corn is threshed — a threshing floor.

FLOOR, v.t. — To lay a floor; to cover with a floor.

The threshing floor of the ancient world was an open, hard, level place, often on a height where the wind could carry off the chaff — which is why the winnowing image and the wind belong together in Scripture.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 15:14 — "Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress: of that wherewith the LORD thy God hath blessed thee thou shalt give unto him."

Ruth 3:6 — "And she went down unto the floor, and did according to all that her mother in law bade her."

Ruth 3:14 — "And she lay at his feet until the morning: and she rose up before one could know another. And he said, Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor."

1 Kings 6:30 — "And the floor of the house he overlaid with gold, within and without."

Matthew 3:12 — "Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire."

Modern Corruption

Matthew 3:12 is corrupted whenever the winnowing is domesticated — the fan made a metaphor for personal refinement rather than a separation of persons — and Ruth 3 whenever the threshingfloor scene is read as a seduction rather than as the careful legal claim it is.

expand to see more

John the Baptist’s sentence has three parts and modern preaching keeps two. The Coming One will purge His floor, gather His wheat into the garner, and burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire. The purging is a separation of persons, not a purification of a single person’s character — the wheat goes one way and the chaff the other, and both destinations are named. Where the figure is softened into a general account of God refining His people, John’s warning is lost, and with it the reason he was preaching repentance to a crowd that thought Abrahamic descent settled the question. The visible church is a threshingfloor: wheat and chaff lie on it together now, and the fan is in a hand already raised.

Ruth 3 requires the opposite correction. The scene is read prurient by modern commentators and preached nervously by those who have absorbed them, but the text itself is scrupulous. Naomi sends Ruth to claim the kinsman-redeemer’s duty; Ruth asks Boaz to spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman; and Boaz answers by blessing her, promising to perform the part of a kinsman, and protecting her reputation before dawn — Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor (Ruth 3:14). Then he goes to the gate and does it legally, in public, before witnesses. The chapter is a model of how a godly man handles a woman’s vulnerability and a legal claim at once: with kindness, with restraint, and in the open.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew goren is a threshingfloor; the Greek halon in Matthew 3:12 is the same, an open threshing area. The English word covers both the household floor and the threshing floor, as the Hebrew and Greek do not.

expand to see more

Hebrew goren (H1637) — a threshingfloor; Deuteronomy 15:14, Ruth 3:3-14, and the floor of Araunah the Jebusite that became the temple site.

Hebrew qarqa' (H7172) — the floor or bottom of a building; the floor of the tabernacle (Numbers 5:17) and of Solomon’s house (1 Kings 6:30).

Greek halon (G257) — a threshingfloor; he will throughly purge his floor (Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17).

Greek ptuon (G4425) — a winnowing fan or fork; the instrument in the Coming One’s hand.

Greek apotheke (G596) — a storehouse, garner; where the wheat is gathered, set against the unquenchable fire for the chaff.

Usage

"Out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress (Deuteronomy 15:14) — the floor as the measure of a man’s increase, and of his liberality."

"Let it not be known that a woman came into the floor (Ruth 3:14) — a redeemer guarding the reputation of the woman he intends to marry."

"He will throughly purge his floor (Matthew 3:12) — the winnowing that separates wheat from chaff, with both destinations named."
